title: How Radioactive Clocks Date Rocks
objective: After this level you can explain how uranium-lead dating gives a rock's age in years and why carbon dating cannot.
summary: Radioactive parent atoms turn into daughters at a steady rate. Zircon takes in uranium but rejects lead, so its lead measures time since it crystallized. Carbon-14 is far too short-lived for rocks.

cards.headline: Tiny zircon crystals carry clocks that started ticking the day they formed.
cards.body: No one was around with a calendar when ancient rocks formed. So how can a geologist say a rock is hundreds of millions of years old? The answer is hidden in its atoms.

cards.headline: An atomic hourglass
cards.body: Some atoms are unstable. A radioactive parent atom, like uranium-238, turns into a daughter atom of another element, like lead-206, at a steady rate. The half-life is the time it takes for half the parent atoms to change. For uranium-238 that's about 4.5 billion years. Measure how much parent is left and how much daughter has built up, and you can calculate how long the clock has been running.

cards.headline: Why zircon makes a perfect clock
cards.body: The trick is knowing the clock started at zero. Zircon crystals take in uranium as they grow but reject lead. So any lead inside a zircon was made by uranium decay after the crystal formed. That's why a radiometric date marks when a rock crystallized from molten rock. Fossils mostly can't be dated this way, so geologists date igneous rock and volcanic ash instead.

cards.fact: Carbon dating is far too short a clock for rocks.
cards.context: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years and is taken up by living things, so radiocarbon dating works only on once-living material from about the past 50,000 years (Chemistry covers how). Rocks millions or billions of years old need slow clocks like uranium.

mascot.line: A classic mix-up: carbon dating is for once-living remains. Ancient rocks get dated with slow clocks like uranium-lead.

cards.headline: Radioactive clocks: read
learned: Parent atoms decay to daughters at a steady rate
Half-life: time for half the parent to decay
Zircon starts with uranium but no lead
Carbon dating is for recent remains, not rocks

questions.prompt: What is a radioactive isotope's half-life?

options.label: Half the age of the rock it sits in
options.rationale: Half-life is a property of the isotope, not the rock.

options.label: The time for half of its parent atoms to decay
The time until all of its atoms have decayed
options.rationale: After one half-life, half the parent atoms remain.

options.label: The halfway point of Earth's history
options.rationale: It depends on the isotope, not on Earth's age.

questions.explanation: Half-life is the time for half of the parent atoms in a sample to turn into daughter atoms.

questions.prompt: How does zircon make uranium-lead dating reliable?

options.label: It soaks up lead from the rocks around it over time
options.rationale: Zircon rejects lead, which is the point.

options.label: It shields its uranium so the atoms stop decaying
options.rationale: Uranium keeps decaying at a steady rate.

options.label: It takes in uranium but rejects lead as it grows
It slowly makes fresh uranium as the crystal ages
options.rationale: Uranium is taken in when the crystal grows.

questions.explanation: A new zircon starts with uranium and almost no lead, so its lead measures how long uranium has been decaying.

questions.prompt: A uranium-lead date on zircon from a granite tells you when what happened?

options.label: The granite's magma cooled and its crystals formed
The granite was weathered and worn down into sand
options.rationale: Weathering doesn't reset the zircon clock.

options.label: The granite was first quarried and dug up by people
options.rationale: The clock started long before anyone found it.

options.label: The granite's plants and animals died
options.rationale: Granite formed from magma, not from living things.

questions.explanation: The clock starts when crystals grow as the magma cools, so the date marks when the granite crystallized.
